Florence, 8 December. After two months of convalescence, Bellini returns to the workshop. Pietro and Davide have secretly prepared an exhibition about the past year. Bellini comes in with his stick and stops in the doorway.
But what have you been up to? If I'd known, I'd have stayed at home another month.
It's an exhibition, professor. It's called "A year of stories". It was set up by the two of us.
It took us three weeks. Each stop tells a moment of the year.
Let's see. First stop: a newspaper. "Caravaggio's secret child discovered by…" Ah, the wrong article!
Yes. Next to it is my letter. The teacher says mistakes must not be hidden: they must be corrected.
And this? A pot with "Not for sale" on it. Davide's cartoon!
According to the paper, the trattoria had reportedly been sold. But Grandma said that if they'd closed it, they'd have had to do it over her dead body.
And this tin box? Don't tell me…
Grandpa's letters. Grandma let us display one. The March one: "I thought you would laugh in my face".
And the last stop? There's only an empty sign.
The last stop is you, professor. The sign says: "He made it". But we wanted you to write it.
Boys… I reckon this time I'm going to get emotional. And don't tell Graziella, or she'll bring me broth here too.

1. Congiuntivo and the sequence of tenses

The congiuntivo appears after: opinions (credo che), wishes (spero che, vorrei che), emotions (sono contento che), doubt (dubito che), conjunctions (benché, affinché, purché, prima che), relative clauses with superlatives (il più bello che…).
Se vieni, ti preparo la ribollita.
Se l’avessi saputo, sarei rimasto a casa.
Never the conditional after "se": NOT "se avrei tempo". Correct: "se avessi tempo".
La mostra è stata allestita dai ragazzi.
Venire ONLY in the simple tenses; in the compound tenses use essere: è stato scoperto (not "è venuto scoperto").
Ha detto che sarebbe tornato il giorno dopo.
Reporting verbs add nuances: affermare, sostenere, ammettere, smentire, precisare (chapter 58).
innanzitutto, inoltre, tuttavia, da un lato… dall’altro, di conseguenza
benché, anche se, pur + gerund, eppure
imperfetto, passato prossimo, passato remoto, trapassato

The idea for the exhibition had come to Davide in mid-October, one evening when he and Pietro were tidying the workshop after the banner. In a drawer they had found everything the year had left behind: the newspaper with the wrong article, the cartoon of the pot, the programme of the Palazzo Vecchio ceremony, the four slips from the fridge with the times of Ion's train, the napkin with the contract signed by the two grandmothers. "It looks like a museum," Pietro had said. Davide had looked at him with shining eyes. "Then let's make one, a museum."

It took them three weeks. They worked on Saturday afternoons and Sunday mornings, when the workshop was closed, with Giulia's permission and the complicity of Chiara, who had promised not to tell the professor. Matei built six plywood panels. Valeria Conti helped them write the labels, "in a register neither too formal nor too informal". Graziella, after long negotiations, allowed a single letter of Aldo's to be displayed, on condition that it was protected by glass and that nobody touched it. Not even the mayor.

The opening date was chosen by Pietro: 8 December. It was the day on which, a year earlier, Chiara had delivered the Prato angel with a fever. And it was also the day the doctors had said Bellini could go back to work, "but only half days, and without lifting anything heavier than a brush". Bellini had protested that his biggest brushes weighed half a kilo. The cardiologist had replied that in that case he would use the small ones.

That morning Bellini arrived in Via Maggio at nine sharp, leaning on a stick he detested, accompanied by Graziella, who wouldn't leave him for a moment. He found the workshop door closed, and on the door a red ribbon. In front of the ribbon were all of them: Giulia with Viola in her arms, Matei, Chiara, Marco, Valeria, Signor Franco with his stationmaster's paddle, Rita, Lorenzo, Mancini with his old voice recorder, even Councillor Neri and the prior of the confraternity with a tray of cantucci. Bellini stopped. "What have you been up to?" he asked.

Pietro handed him a pair of scissors. "You have to cut it, professor. You're opening it." Bellini cut the ribbon with a slightly trembling hand, and the door opened. Inside, the workshop was unrecognisable. The tables had been pushed against the walls, and in the middle six panels formed a spiral route. Above the entrance was a banner painted by Davide: "A year of stories — 1st edition". Underneath, in small letters: "Free entry. Please do not touch. Especially the letter."

The first stop was called "March: Totò on the front page". There was the article with the three mistakes, framed, and next to it Pietro's letter to the editor. The label, written by Valeria, said: "The child's face was not discovered by Ernesto Bellini, but by Giulia and Matei. The painting has never been moved and never will be. Mistakes, as Pietro's teacher says, must not be hidden: they must be corrected." Underneath, Davide had drawn Totò winking. Bellini read everything, then laughed. "My grandfather, on the front page," he said. "He'd have loved it to bits."

The second stop was "April and May: Via Maggio is not for sale". There was the printed agency report, with the conditional underlined in red: "avrebbe acquistato", "sarebbero previsti". There were Davide's cartoons, the photo of the contract signed with the gold pen, and a sentence of Bellini's own, taken from the meeting: "A neighbourhood without residents is a painting without a face." Bellini stopped in front of his own sentence and cleared his throat. "I didn't remember saying it so well," he admitted. "I must have had a good audience."

The third stop, "June: Chinese whispers", made everyone laugh. There were the four slips from the fridge, with the four different times, hung in a row like paintings, and a label written by Pietro in reported speech: "Grandma Doina said they would arrive on Saturday. Dad Matei said the party was on Friday. Signor Franco said it depended on where they changed. The fruit seller said to bring strawberries. They were all right, except Dad." Matei protested that he wasn't Pietro's dad. Pietro replied that, for the purposes of the exhibition, he was everybody's dad.

The fourth stop was the quietest. It was called "July: the letters in the attic". In the middle, under glass, was the March 1974 letter, in Aldo's slightly faded handwriting. Next to it was the tin box with the lady and the parasol, closed. And underneath, a one-line label Graziella had insisted on writing herself: "I thought he had never seen me. I was wrong." Bellini stood in front of the glass for a long time. Graziella, beside him, looked the other way. Neither of them said anything. There was no need.

The fifth stop was the most colourful: "August: the grandmothers' contest". There was the napkin with the contract, with everyone's signatures and Lupino's paw print. There was a photo of the two grandmothers under the umbrella, Graziellina and Assuntina, eating watermelon and laughing. And there was Pietro's list of false alterations, with Davide's drawings: the giant madman, the enormous barrel, the angry turkey. The prior of the confraternity, who didn't know the story, asked why there was a turkey in a restoration workshop. They explained the grammar to him. He said he preferred cantucci.

Next to the fifth stop, on a tablet propped against a chair, a video started every five minutes. It was Grandma Assunta, from Naples, sitting in her kitchen with her stick leaning against the table, speaking while looking slightly too high, like someone not used to cameras. "Dear professor," she said, "they tell me you've had a little problem with your heart. I'm so sorry. If I'd been younger, I'd have come to Florence with a ragù. But the boys asked me to tell you just one thing, and I'll tell you: look after yourself, because at a certain age the heart must be treated like a pot of ragù. Low heat, patience, and never leave it alone." Then she winked at the camera and added: "Greetings to Graziellina." Every time the video started again, Graziella pretended not to hear. But she stayed nearby all morning.

The sixth stop was "September: the banner". There was a big photo of the procession, with the prior bowing in front of the trattoria, and next to it Pietro's shift board, covered in names, times and coffee stains, with Chiara's red words at the bottom: "We made it." And then, after the sixth stop, there was one last panel, small, almost hidden, with a white sign. On the sign was written only: "December". Underneath, nothing. And next to it, hanging on a string, a black marker.

"And this?" asked Bellini. Davide, who until then had stayed in the background, stepped forward. "The last stop is you, professor," he said. "The title was going to be 'He made it'. But we thought it would be better if you wrote it. In your own hand. Because it's you who made it, not us." There was a long silence. Bellini looked at the white sign, then at the marker, then at the boys. Mancini, without a sound, switched on his recorder.

Bellini took the marker. But instead of writing "I made it", he stood thinking for a moment, and then wrote something else, slowly, with a trembling hand, in the neat handwriting of someone who has spent his life retouching details. When he had finished, he stepped aside so everyone could read: "December: we made it. If it hadn't been for you, I wouldn't have made it. A year ago I thought the workshop needed me. Today I know that I needed the workshop. And you. And the broth."

Graziella was the first to clap, and the first to cry, in that order. Then everyone clapped, and the prior of the confraternity, moved, handed out cantucci without counting the five minutes. Viola, in Giulia's arms, clapped her little hands and said her favourite word of the year: "Figo!" Councillor Neri went up to Mancini and asked him quietly if he had recorded everything. Mancini nodded. "Tomorrow," he said, "this is the front page. I've already written the headline: 'The professor returns. And says thank you'."

Later, when the crowd had gone and the workshop was quiet again, Bellini sat down at his old table in the corner for the first time in three months. In front of him was the black notebook Graziella had confiscated in hospital and had now given back to him. He opened it at the last written page, the one about the banner. Then he turned the page and wrote the date: 8 December. Underneath, he wrote a single line: "Today a year has ended. I've learned more from the boys than they have from me."

Pietro and Davide, who were taking down the banner, saw him writing. Pietro tiptoed over and read over his shoulder. Then he said, in the tone of a strict teacher: "Professor, there's a mistake. 'I've learned more from the boys than they have from me.' It's correct, but it's too modest. It needs a subjunctive." Bellini looked up, amused. "And which subjunctive, teacher?" Pietro thought about it. "Like this: 'I hope the boys have learned from me at least half of what I've learned from them.'"

Bellini laughed heartily, as he hadn't laughed for months. Then he crossed out the line and rewrote it exactly as Pietro had said, word for word, with the past subjunctive in the right place. Underneath he added: "Correction suggested by Pietro, aged 12, who now speaks better than I do. And by Davide, aged 13, who draws better than anyone." Davide blushed to the tips of his ears. Pietro, on the other hand, looked at the page with professional satisfaction. "Now it's right," he said. "Now it's perfect."

That evening, at the trattoria, there was the end-of-year dinner. It wasn't Christmas yet, but Graziella said you celebrate when there's a reason, not when the calendar says so. There was ribollita with Sorrento oil, broth for Bellini "just in case", the prior's cantucci and a cake from Lorenzo with the words "Welcome back". When it was time for the toast, Matei stood up and said he wanted to review the year, the way newspapers do. Everyone protested that it was too long. So Matei did it in a single sentence.

"On the one hand," he said, raising his glass, "it was a year in which the paper wrote badly about us, our home was nearly sold, the professor gave us a terrible fright and two grandmothers nearly went to war. On the other hand, if none of this had happened, we would never have known how good we are at getting by together." Bellini raised his glass of water, the only one the cardiologist allowed him. "In conclusion," he added, "we made it. And next year, God willing, we'll make it again." Viola, from her high chair, raised her spoon. "Figo," she said. And for once nobody corrected her.
